prompt:
Propose one numerical repair for f(x)=log(1-exp(-x)) and its first
derivative for positive finite float32/float64 scalar x with normal-range results.
The textbook loss and exp(-x)/(1-exp(-x)) derivative can lose significant digits.
The Softmax lesson is to preserve small quantities in the actual arithmetic;
finite output or a correct-looking forward value does not verify the derivative.
Return only a JSON object with exactly program and explanation. explanation is a
nonempty string. program has exactly loss and gradient expression nodes.
Leaves: {"input":"x"} or {"const":finite_number} (no booleans).
Operators: {"op":name,"args":[nodes]}; unary neg/exp/expm1/log/log1p;
binary add/sub/mul/div/le; ternary where(boolean,number,number), evaluated lazily.
Only le produces booleans. Both outputs must be numeric. All arithmetic retains
the input dtype. No Python, code fences, imports, paths or external tools.
Whole response <=32768 UTF-8 bytes, program <=256 nodes and depth <=16.
This is a public development task, not a scientific novelty or held-out claim.

External known-method context and public development feedback follow.
Use these as sourced input; their presence does not establish discovery or correctness.
Externally authored known-method summaries (not discovered by this model):

[log1mexp-piecewise] https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/Rmpfr/html/log1mexp.html
For positive x, f(x)=log(1-exp(-x)). Mächler's documented stable method uses loss=log(-expm1(-x)) when x<=log(2), and loss=log1p(-exp(-x)) otherwise. log(2)=0.6931471805599453. The minus sign before expm1(-x) is essential: its result is negative. EIDOS analytic derivation: the positive first derivative can be written exp(-x)/(-expm1(-x)). This derivative identity is derived here, not attributed to the Rmpfr documentation. Preserve the input dtype; evaluate the selected loss branch lazily. Scope: the declared positive float32/float64 public normal-result domain, not subnormals, higher derivatives or training outcomes. This supplies a known repair, not a new discovery.

[log1p-small] https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.log1p.html
NumPy log1p(y) computes log(1+y) accurately for small real y even when forming 1+y would round to one. Its real finite domain requires y>-1. For large positive x, y=-exp(-x) is a small negative increment. Using log1p does not by itself verify the derivative, input dtype or validity at every branch boundary.

campaign_request.text:
Externally authored known-method summaries (not discovered by this model):

[log1mexp-piecewise] https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/Rmpfr/html/log1mexp.html
For positive x, f(x)=log(1-exp(-x)). Mächler's documented stable method uses loss=log(-expm1(-x)) when x<=log(2), and loss=log1p(-exp(-x)) otherwise. log(2)=0.6931471805599453. The minus sign before expm1(-x) is essential: its result is negative. EIDOS analytic derivation: the positive first derivative can be written exp(-x)/(-expm1(-x)). This derivative identity is derived here, not attributed to the Rmpfr documentation. Preserve the input dtype; evaluate the selected loss branch lazily. Scope: the declared positive float32/float64 public normal-result domain, not subnormals, higher derivatives or training outcomes. This supplies a known repair, not a new discovery.

[log1p-small] https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.log1p.html
NumPy log1p(y) computes log(1+y) accurately for small real y even when forming 1+y would round to one. Its real finite domain requires y>-1. For large positive x, y=-exp(-x) is a small negative increment. Using log1p does not by itself verify the derivative, input dtype or validity at every branch boundary.

task_prompt:
Propose one numerical repair for f(x)=log(1-exp(-x)) and its first
derivative for positive finite float32/float64 scalar x with normal-range results.
The textbook loss and exp(-x)/(1-exp(-x)) derivative can lose significant digits.
The Softmax lesson is to preserve small quantities in the actual arithmetic;
finite output or a correct-looking forward value does not verify the derivative.
Return only a JSON object with exactly program and explanation. explanation is a
nonempty string. program has exactly loss and gradient expression nodes.
Leaves: {"input":"x"} or {"const":finite_number} (no booleans).
Operators: {"op":name,"args":[nodes]}; unary neg/exp/expm1/log/log1p;
binary add/sub/mul/div/le; ternary where(boolean,number,number), evaluated lazily.
Only le produces booleans. Both outputs must be numeric. All arithmetic retains
the input dtype. No Python, code fences, imports, paths or external tools.
Whole response <=32768 UTF-8 bytes, program <=256 nodes and depth <=16.
